segments.text: Thank you, Mr. Loeschel. Up next is Aaron Spiegel.

Good afternoon, Chairwoman Carrasco, members of the committee. My name is Rabbi Aaron Spiegel. I'm with the Greater Indianapolis Multifaith Alliance, and we stand in opposition to SB 285. My testimony on the House version of a similar bill last year focused on the origins of this type of legislation coming from a Texas -based special interest group that believes on a one -size -fits -all solution to homelessness. The Cicero Group's philosophy of services first is now a national priority, and I've seen firsthand that our homeless neighbors are suffering because of it. Unfortunately, there's no one answer to this solution to this problem. And through my years of experience working with the homeless populations and organizations that are trying to help, I've learned that homelessness is a local, sometimes hyper -local, issue that needs resources rather than laws that tie the hands of local communities while not actually solving the root of the problem. I'd offer that the state's place in ending homelessness is not legislating best practices, because without providing local resources, local communities with the tools, resources, and flexibility to do what's best, we're not going to address the problem. Local government is the closest level of government to the people, and more importantly, the level through which homeless people acquire assistance. The state should resource them to innovate and experiment. If communities are given these tools and they determine that what's best for them is a ban on camping, then so be it. And let them address that for their community. But I can say with certainty that banning camping, public camping in Indianapolis, will harm the strides we are making at solving chronic homelessness. Streets to Home Indy is a community -driven initiative to provide permanent housing and supportive services for the chronically homeless and is a collaborative public -private partnership. It's working, and it can work for other communities in Indiana. There's more than 20 years of data that shows that the solution to homelessness is housing. And the only direct causation for homelessness is a lack of affordable housing. And

the only direct proven solution is permanent housing. Shelters, encampments, transitional temporary housing do nothing but move people around so we don't have to see them anymore, and even that's temporary. Encampments don't help, shelters don't help, and putting the homeless into the justice system just doesn't help. I regularly hear a version of, well, it's better that they're in jail or in the justice system than they're on the street. Let me share with you that in November, at a downtown church in Indianapolis at a Thanksgiving meal, Pastor David Green of Concerned Clergy and I did a town hall meeting for the homeless community so they could learn about Streets to Home. The thing they wanted to talk about more than anything else was the possibility of being arrested for sleeping on the street. As my friend Billy said, why do they want to make our lives worse? The second biggest theme of conversation was why they don't want to go to the shelters. One neighbor commented, the shelters are just plain scary. We're forced to sleep in a room with 50 guys, sometimes I'm on the floor, people steal my stuff, and the staff can't control the fights. Expecting a homeless person to pay a fine makes them even more vulnerable. It makes what little they have even less so. And they are terrified of law enforcement. Let me repeat, they are terrified of law enforcement. Being arrested just destroys what dignity they have left. All our faith traditions have some version created in the image of God. Whether one believes that or not, it's not lost on me that every faith tradition has some version of this universal truth. Inequality is an innate human condition. All our faith traditions have the mandate to take care of the least among us. How we treat the weakest in our midst is at the core of our humanity. Through Indianapolis' Streets to Home India initiative, the faith community of Indianapolis has made clear that we've reclaimed the moral and ethical mandate to take care of our most vulnerable. We stand unified in our belief that putting homeless people in the criminal justice system is not part of the solution. In fact, it perpetuates the never -ending cycle that puts these most vulnerable people in an even more dangerous, and financially devastating position. So I ask you to listen with both your heads and your hearts. Let's not temporarily clear the streets in order to clear our consciences. We are eager to work with you to find other opportunities in addressing this issue that is so important to us. Thank you so much.
Thank you, Rabbi Spiegel. Up next is Lasima Packett.
Please introduce yourself and let us know if you're here representing anyone.
All right. Up next is Rachel Sample from the Indianapolis Foundation.
Welcome, Ms. Sample. Thank you. Good afternoon.

Thank you for letting me be here today. My name is Rachel Sample and I am the Housing Senior Community Leadership Officer at the Indianapolis Foundation. The mission of the foundation is to create a community where everyone can thrive, regardless of race, place, or identity. Last year, our organization granted nearly $1 million in housing and homeless services grants in Marion County in addition to administering the Housing to Recovery Fund, the largest public -private fund for supportive services in the state. We are also a major funder of the Indianapolis Streets to Home Initiative. As a key partner in the Streets to Home Initiative, we have seen its work firsthand. We hear that senators are concerned about the conditions of folks living in encampments and on the street, and so are we. Our unsheltered neighbors are not choosing to live outside. Streets to Home demonstrates that when someone is offered a real housing solution, they are housed at a rate of 92%. However, the journey to housing is not straightforward and is important to address the barriers to housing stability and prioritize affordable housing. Affordable and safe housing in Indiana is a crisis. According to the National Low Income Housing Coalition, Indiana has only 38 affordable units for every very low -income household. Almost 75 % of very low -income households are paying more than 50 % of their income to housing. In the last decade, rents in Indiana have increased by 52%, outpacing wage growth significantly. We observe this problem when we see our neighbors sleeping outside. Indiana's solution to the crisis of unsheltered homelessness should be an investment in affordable housing and services, not in creating barriers to accessing resources. I'm here to testify in opposition of SB 285. During my career, I have overseen the Continuum of Care program. Recipients of these grants already are required to report their performance annually. Staff at the City of Indianapolis and the Indiana Housing Community Development Authority are reviewing this data. Additional reporting requirements for COC recipients described in SB 285 are redundant and at a minimum. This is an administrative burden. Trust and collaboration are key to serving our unsheltered neighbors. Outreach workers, local government, and law enforcement partner together in this work every day. SB 285 will place law enforcement in a position to cite and find individuals eliminating trust and relationships both with our unsheltered neighbors and outreach workers. We should support stronger partnerships. Indianapolis' Streets to Home Initiative is an example of how investment alongside partnership addresses unsheltered homelessness. I was recently discussing the issue of criminal history as a barrier to housing with Streets to Home team members. In 2025, the Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana reported that Indianapolis rental vacancy is extremely low at 3 .9%, which means landlords can be very selective in screening tenants, including criminal history. If SB 285 became law, folks served by Streets to Home could face more difficulties in obtaining and maintaining housing. Our focus should be on policies that expand access to housing with services. This is the housing -first approach, and Indianapolis Foundation's Housing to Recovery Fund is a model of its success. Since 2021, Housing to Recovery Fund has invested more than $8 million in nonprofit partners serving 500 individuals. With this investment, 95 % of households remain housed and obtain health insurance. 88 % of the households engaged in the program access physical, behavioral, and behavioral health appointments. When an individual has the stability of home, they have the capacity to address their issues. In addition, housing to recovery funds with mental or physical health. Our approach is also cost -effective. The Housing to Recovery Fund cost for supportive services is approximately $9 ,000 per person per year. It is an estimated that a person living on the street in our community costs upwards of $30 ,000 in public services, such as police runs, emergency room visits, or jail stays. The requirements of this bill could compound these public costs. Indianapolis Foundation is here as a partner to seek policies to expand access to housing across the state and in our community, not limited. The state's current budget provides zero dollars in dedicated resources to address homelessness. And if we want to end unsheltered homelessness in our state, this must change. Street -to -home models should be available in every county, not just one. I encourage this committee to deliberate on solutions to homelessness that are proven to address this crisis. And the Foundation is here to be a partner in seeking those solutions. Thank you for your time.
Thank you very much, Ms. Sample. Up next, is Chelsea Hearing -Cosey. Did I get that right? Yeah. Great. Thank so much.

Awesome. Thank you so much. Good afternoon, Chairman Carrasco and committee members. Thank you for allowing me to speak today on this important issue and state our position in opposition to SB 285. My name is Lauren Murphy. I'm a policy analyst with the Indiana Community Action Poverty Institute. Hoosiers we serve have told us in no uncertain terms that housing is a major community need. Many are just one or two paychecks away from homelessness. As one Hoosier shared with us, being poor is expensive, as it's costing me financially and mentally going from motel to motel, not being able to save. SB 285, and in particular the misdemeanor charge, Class C, would push those already experiencing homelessness further into poverty, create additional barriers to obtaining housing, and place those who are at risk of homelessness into a place of fear. We had a person reach out to us concerned about what would happen to her and her 80 -year -old mother if she lost housing, became unhoused, and had no access to services in her area. Would they go to jail? She was worried. While it may appear simple to simply direct those experiencing homelessness to shelters or other services, this fails to recognize the limited resources that presently exist across our state. When looking at just mental health and behavioral health services in our state, the IU Bowen Center's 2014 study found that all 92 counties in Indiana were federally designated as mental health care provider shortage areas. The minimum number required for meeting the provider ratio that is not deemed a shortage is one provider for every 30 ,000 people. We are not even meeting that threshold. When looking at even space that we have to house those who are experiencing homelessness in our state, the present total balance of state continued care, this is only 91 counties, not including Marion County, inventory count as of 2025, point in time period, was 80 % bed capacity was filled. We do not have enough services presently to meet the current needs. Instead of the approaches suggested in this bill, which focus on the actions of those in -house and not the root causes, we can and should focus on services, good pay and stable jobs, affordable housing, mental health supports, and supports for those who fall behind on bills or face evictions, which can protect Hoosiers from being pushed into poverty. I hope the committee will instead consider creating and supporting legislation that would support the homeless service providers that work in our state and collaborate with them, and ensure we have enough resources to support our unhoused and unsheltered neighbors before implementing any proposed changes in this bill. Assist in empowering Hoosiers who are low income and are at risk of experiencing homelessness by investing in trusted and effective housing support providers to ensure they can innovate to meet local needs is another approach. Hoosiers are hardworking, but all it could take is a bad illness, an unexpected expensive car repair, or other significant costs that throw many of them into homelessness. We need investment in people and stability. We can be responsible and responsive by crafting solutions that get people housed and on a path to self -sufficiency and align ourselves with our values as Hoosiers by showing care for our fellow neighbors in need.
